title: A hard conversation
hookLine: Plato froze with his hand raised: the Stoics' jolt, the delay, and Epictetus's other handle
tomorrow: why would a holy man squeeze bread until it bled?

cards: A raised hand, frozen in the air. The Roman writer Seneca tells this story about Plato.
A slave in Plato's house had done something wrong, and Plato, angry, ordered him to bare his shoulders for a beating, meaning to strike him with his own hand. He lifted the hand.
Then he stopped, and stood there, hand still up, like a statue of a man about to hit someone. A friend walked in and asked what he was doing. Plato said he was punishing an angry man.
He meant himself. Another time, Seneca adds, Plato handed an offending slave over to a friend to deal with, because, he said, I am angry.

teach.h: THE GREATEST REMEDY FOR ANGER: DELAY.
teach.b: Seneca tells it in his book On Anger, and he draws the lesson plainly: the greatest remedy for anger is delay.

teach.h: THE JOLT ARRIVES ON ITS OWN.
teach.b: Seneca was a Stoic, and the Stoics taught that the first sting arrives on its own: the heat in the face, the jolt. That part isn't chosen, and Plato never pretended he wasn't angry.
What comes next is: the judgment, this is an insult, this is unbearable, and then the act. Delay is the gap between. Epictetus, another Stoic teacher, gives the gap a job.
In his Handbook he says everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it can't.

teach.h: HE IS YOUR BROTHER: LIFT THAT ONE.
teach.b: If your brother wrongs you, don't pick it up by the handle that he wronged you; that one can't be carried. Pick it up by the other: he is your brother, raised with you. The wrong is still a wrong.
You choose which side to lift.
That's the Stoic teaching in three beats: the jolt, the delay, the other handle. It isn't swallowing the hard conversation. It's holding it so you can actually have it.

how: Readers of the Stoics practice the pause Seneca recommends, waiting before they speak or act in anger, and use Epictetus's two handles to look for the side of a conflict they can bear.

o: a formal review meeting with your manager and HR
an argument you win by staying completely silent
a talk where the jolt comes before you choose your next move

games.q: the jolt, the delay, the handle: tap the pairs.
p: froze with his hand in the air
the greatest remedy for anger is delay

s: the Stoics teach you to feel nothing when you're wronged
Seneca expects the jolt. what he asks for is delay before the judgment and the act.
Plato stopped because his friend talked him out of it
he stopped himself, mid-strike, once he saw he was angry. the friend walked in after.
Epictetus says the handle 'he wronged me' can't be carried
that handle can't be borne. the other one, he is your brother, can.

games.q: your brother borrows your car and returns it with the tank empty, again. you're about to text him. what would Epictetus lift?
o: the other handle: he's your brother. then say the hard thing about the tank.
the handle that he wronged you, so he finally feels how unfair it is.
neither: say nothing, since a real Stoic just lets it go forever.
games.why: everything has two handles. Epictetus doesn't erase the wrong; he picks it up by the side you can carry, so the talk can happen.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, the opposite of a raised hand. Bring to mind one hard conversation you're facing, and for a few breaths let the jolt be there without doing anything with it.
Then look for its other handle: one true thing about that person you can carry.

wordCard.voice: A hard conversation: the jolt comes on its own; the delay and the handle you lift are yours. The Stoics' way through it.

orig.note: Latin: delay. Seneca's remedy for anger, in his book On Anger.

carryVoice: Your line: the other handle. The wrong stays a wrong, and the person stays a person. That's three days into work.
